query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Atomic-level disorder in equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles creates significant local variations in bonding strength and lattice strain, which in turn broadens and spatially heterogenizes the premelting regime compared to chemically simpler, more homogeneous bimetallic nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles; baseline particles are bimetallic nanoparticles (e.g., Fe–Co) of similar size and dispersion.
generation.intervention: Application of in situ thermal microscopy during controlled heating to record spatially resolved phase-transition behavior.
generation.conditions: Identical heating rates applied over a temperature range covering the onset of premelting through complete melting, for nanoparticles in the 5–50 nm size regime under high-temperature conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Local variations in atomic configurations and bond strengths induced by high configurational entropy.
generation.mechanism: The multi-element disorder in HEA nanoparticles leads to regions with differing bonding environments and local strain. These variations result in lower and spatially varied melting onset temperatures, as opposed to the uniform melting behavior observed in bimetallic nanoparticles with simpler, homogeneous bonding networks.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under controlled heating, HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a broader premelting interval with spatially heterogeneous melting (with different regions beginning to melt at different temperatures), whereas baseline bimetallic nanoparticles will show a sharper, more uniform melting transition.
generation.baseline: Bimetallic nanoparticles (e.g., Fe–Co) with simpler chemistry, expected to have a uniform and narrowly-defined melting transition.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoparticles where surface effects are significant (typically 5–50 nm in diameter) and under thermal conditions that allow observation of premelting phenomena. It is especially pertinent during high-temperature synthesis and rapid cooling regimes that consolidate solid solutions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise extent and temperature range of melting heterogeneity in HEA nanoparticles may be influenced by synthesis conditions, particle size distribution, and defect densities, which could add variability to the observed effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ high-temperature thermal microscopy on two identically synthesized sets of nanoparticles: one set of equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles and one set of baseline bimetallic nanoparticles (e.g., Fe–Co). Monitor the onset and spatial progression of premelting and melting within individual particles.
measurements: Temperature mapping of melting onset across different regions within single nanoparticles
Statistical distribution of melting temperatures for each nanoparticle type
Comparative analysis of the homogeneity versus heterogeneity in melting behavior between the HEA and bimetallic samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA nanoparticles do not exhibit a broader, spatially heterogeneous premelting transition (i.e., if their melting behavior is similar in sharpness and uniformity to that of the baseline bimetallic nanoparticles), then the hypothesis linking atomic-level disorder to extended, heterogeneous premelting is falsified.

Here, we propose a fabrication method applicable to both equiatomic and non-equiatomic HEAs, where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. The alloy solidifies and recrystallizes into a single-phase FCC polycrystal. This unique non-equiatomic alloy can be utilized for fundamental studies by evaluating the equiatomic counterpart and emphasizing concepts related to composition-microstructure-property relations. This is evidenced by the duplex structure that remains partitioned after high-temperature annealing. AbstractThe single-step incorporation of multiple immiscible elements into colloidal high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles has manifold technological potential, but it continues to be a challenge for state-of-the-art synthesis methods. Hence, the development of a synthesis approach by which the chemical composition and phase of colloidal HEA nanoparticles can be controlled could lead to a new pool of nanoalloys with unparalleled functionalities. Herein, this study reports the single-step synthesis of colloidal CoCrFeMnNi HEA nanoparticles with targeted equimolar stoichiometry and diameters less than 5 nm by liquid-phase, ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation of the consolidated and heat-treated micropowders of the five constituent metals. Further, the scalability of the process with an unprecedented productivity of 3 grams of colloidal HEA nanoparticles per hour is demonstrated. Electrochemical analysis reveals a unique redox behavior of the particles' surfaces in an alkaline environment and a potential for future application as a heterogeneous catalyst for the oxygen evolution reaction. frame.goal: To elucidate the governing physics of the nanoscale premelting and melting behavior of chemically complex high-entropy alloys, specifically how atomic-level disorder and bonding variations influence phase transitions compared to simpler nanoparticle systems.
frame.limitation: Limited understanding of the thermal response of these high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles, stemming from sparse research on chemically complex systems and the inherent variability introduced by multiple elemental constituents, which constrains the interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis processes.

decision.trend: Initial work on single‐metal nanoparticles (e.g., Ag, Au, Al, Pd) showed relatively sharp, uniform melting transitions. Subsequent studies on bimetallic nanoparticles revealed that introducing a second element can lead to varied atomic configurations and bond-strength mismatches, resulting in broadened or spatially heterogeneous premelting and melting behavior. More recent, though sparse, investigations of high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles—exemplified by in‐situ studies (PMC8320920) and high‐temperature laser-synthesis methods (PMC9064730)—indicate that the enhanced chemical complexity further reinforces local variations in atomic bonding. This suggests that atomic-level disorder may be key in governing the onset and the progression of the phase transition, yet a quantitative mechanistic link remains to be established.
decision.unsolved: It remains unsolved how exactly the configurational entropy caused by multi-element disorder alters local melting dynamics; in particular, how variations in local bonding strengths within a single high-entropy nanoparticle lead to an extended, spatially heterogeneous premelting regime compared to the more uniform behavior seen in simpler systems.
decision.lever: In situ thermal microscopy (or similar spatially resolved high-temperature characterization) comparing the onset and progression of premelting in equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles versus a baseline (e.g., a bimetallic nanoparticle with similar size and comparable surface area) under identical heating rates.
decision.why: This approach directly tests the hypothesis that atomic-level disorder in high-entropy alloys induces locally varied bond-strengths, causing a broader and spatially heterogeneous phase transition. Prior trends indicate that increased compositional complexity leads to non-uniform melting behavior, making a controlled comparison under identical thermal conditions a decisive experiment—if the HEA nanoparticles exhibit significant spatial variability in the onset of melting relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is supported; if not, it would decisively falsify the mechanism.
